content: In one study, data from male and female participants consuming whole milk and heat-treated cow’s milk were combined. For three studies, formula groups were combined. In two studies, standard deviations from studies with similar populations and sample sizes were used. Annex 4 provides further details on studies where data were converted for this review. Four studies included co-interventions. In one study, infants in the cow’s milk feeding group consumed iron-fortified cereal daily, while another study had both the cow’s milk and formula feeding groups consume iron-fortified cereal daily. One study provided all infants with a supplement containing ascorbic acid, iron from ferrous sulfate, and fluoride from sodium fluoride. Another study provided infants fed cow’s milk with a supplement of ascorbic acid and fluoride in the form of sodium fluoride, while the formula group received a daily supplement of fluoride only. Four studies (one randomized controlled trial [RCT] and three observational studies) included confounding variables in their analysis. One study from the United Kingdom randomized infants from the Indian subcontinent separately due to the high risk of iron deficiency in this population. This study adjusted for variables such as breastfeeding, median breastfeeding duration, first child status, maternal education, and non-manual social class for neurodevelopmental outcomes expressed as Bayley Psychomotor Development Index (PDI). A prospective cohort study adjusted for maternal education, smoking during pregnancy, and parity as confounding variables for mean weight. Another cohort study used multiple regression analysis to test associations between hemoglobin, serum ferritin, mean corpuscular volume, transferrin saturation, and transferrin as dependent variables, and demographic and dietary factors, growth, and morbidity as independent variables. One cohort study used a linear model adjusted for gender, birth weight, and length of exclusive breastfeeding. Two observational studies did not adjust for any confounding variables. The meta-analysis and GRADE analysis results for primary outcomes and selected secondary outcomes at the longest follow-up are reported. Results for primary outcomes at other follow-up durations, such as 7, 9, and 12 months, are available. GRADE evidence profiles for primary and selected secondary outcomes are shown. All included studies contributed data to an outcome for meta-analysis, except for two cohort studies where data were reported in a way that could not be meta-analyzed. Results for these studies were reported individually. For anemia at the longest follow-up, two RCTs and two cohort studies reported data. Each study used slightly different definitions of anemia. Data from the two cohort studies included 327 participants, with 155 in the milk feeding group and 172 in the formula feeding group. Data from the two RCTs included 209 participants, with 60 in the milk feeding group and 149 in the formula feeding group. Three studies had the longest follow-up time of 12 months, while one study had a follow-up time of 18 months. The GRADE certainty of evidence was downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, as all studies were conducted in high-income countries. Subgroup analyses based on country type, type of animal milk, and type of feeding in the comparison group were not performed, as all studies were conducted in high-income countries and used cow’s milk as the animal milk. A subgroup analysis based on the age of initiation did not show significant differences between groups at 7 and 9 months of age. Sensitivity analysis based on the type of model used showed consistent results for fixed versus random models of meta-analysis. One cohort study had a high risk of bias due to a lack of adjustment for confounding variables. Two studies reported data on gastrointestinal blood loss. One was a cohort study with 81 participants, and the other was an RCT with 43 participants. The results showed very low to low certainty of evidence that cow’s milk leads to increased gastrointestinal blood loss. The GRADE certainty was downgraded due to risk of bias, imprecision, and indirectness. Three RCTs reported weight-for-age outcomes, including 556 participants. Two studies had a follow-up time of 12 months, and one had a follow-up time of 18 months. The GRADE certainty of evidence was low due to risk of bias and indirectness. Two RCTs reported length-for-age outcomes, including 529 participants. The GRADE certainty of evidence was also low for similar reasons. No studies reported data on weight-for-length. Three RCTs and two cohort studies reported data on blood hemoglobin concentration. The cohort studies included 246 participants, and the RCTs included 250 participants. The GRADE certainty of evidence was low due to risk of bias and indirectness. Two cohort studies reported data on iron deficiency anemia, including 327 participants. The GRADE certainty of evidence was low due to risk of bias and indirectness. Four studies reported data on serum ferritin levels, including one cohort study and three RCTs. The cohort study included 165 participants. One study reported data on triglyceride levels, and one study reported data on allergies as IgE levels. No studies reported data on pneumonia, obesity, or overweight. One study reported that the duration of cow’s milk feeding decreased hemoglobin levels by 2 g/L for every month of feeding. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of animal milk versus infant formula as the main milk drink for non-breastfed or mixed-fed infants aged 6–11 months. The evidence suggests that the use of animal milk compared to infant formula may increase the risk of anemia and gastrointestinal blood loss and decrease blood hemoglobin and serum ferritin levels. However, the evidence for growth outcomes was of low certainty, and no conclusive statements could be made regarding neurodevelopmental outcomes or adverse events such as constipation and diarrhea. The findings are limited to cow’s milk and cannot be generalized to other types of animal milk. Further studies are needed to explore the effects of fortified cow’s milk and complementary feedings on anemia risk.
